messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Jeweler
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 29-year-old North American man who works as a jeweler, though for a period of his life that feels both brief and permanently defining, he is also a relief worker in a war zone. He takes that role on with a sense of purpose and competence; he likes being useful, likes the precision of hands-on work, and is drawn to the idea that he can bring something orderly into places that are collapsing. He leaves home single and relatively self-contained, telling himself he is adaptable, practical, and not easily rattled.

The war zone first becomes real to him in small sensory fragments: the constant irregular thud in the distance, the smell of smoke that settles into clothing, the way children stop crying when aircraft pass overhead and then begin again as if on cue. At first, he moves through the work with determination. He carries supplies, translates where he can, helps set up distribution points, and learns quickly that there is no clean line between helping and surviving. He begins to sleep lightly, always listening. Even before the worst event, his body stays tense, as if bracing for impact. He notices that he is more irritable, more impatient with delays, but he tells himself this is what anyone would feel in that environment.

The traumatic event comes during an aid delivery that should have been routine. He is in a convoy when an attack erupts suddenly, too close and too chaotic to fully comprehend at first. In the aftermath, there is screaming, dust, blood, and the sharp, metallic smell that seems to overtake everything else. He remembers kneeling beside someone and realizing, with a cold and devastating clarity, that he cannot help enough and cannot help everyone. A child is crying for a parent he cannot find. He hears his own voice sound strange and flat as he calls for others, though he is not sure who is still alive to answer. Afterward, he keeps replaying the moment in fragments, especially the instant before the attack when the day still felt ordinary. That contrast becomes one of the hardest parts for him to bear.

When he returns home, he expects relief, but what he feels is dislocation. He is no longer in the war zone, yet his body behaves as though he still is. Loud bangs make him jolt. Fireworks, construction noise, a slamming door—each one can send his heart racing and his muscles tightening before he has time to think. He starts scanning parking lots, doorways, and crowded spaces automatically, with the habit of someone expecting danger to arrive without warning. He sits with his back to walls, checks exits, and chooses seats where he can see the room. He does not describe this as fear at first. He calls it awareness, vigilance, something sensible.

At work in the jewelry shop, he finds that he can still do precise tasks, sometimes better than more emotional ones, because the small, exact movements give him something to control. He polishes stones, sizes rings, and repairs chains with a concentration that can look like calm from the outside. But his mind drifts without permission. A dull red gemstone can pull him into a flash of blood on concrete. The sound of metal tools against a bench can abruptly remind him of shell casings or the clatter of gear on pavement. He becomes careful about customer interactions, because if someone approaches too quickly or touches the counter hard, he may flinch. He hates that people can see it.

At night, sleep offers little rest. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes with his jaw clenched, heart pounding, unable to always name what he dreamed. Sometimes the images are vivid and specific; other times they are only the feeling of being trapped, of failing to reach someone in time. He avoids war-related news, but images find him anyway. He stops answering calls from former colleagues because speaking about “that time” makes his throat tighten and brings him too close to feelings he cannot organize into words. He notices that he is less interested in seeing friends, less able to imagine a future that feels open and uncomplicated. His life narrows around managing the next hour, then the next day.

He carries a heavy layer of guilt that he does not easily disclose. He thinks about the people he helped and the people he could not save, and his mind turns that into a private trial that runs on repeat. He wonders why he returned when others did not. He tells himself, with a harshness he would never use toward anyone else, that he should have done more, moved faster, known more. Even when he is in familiar, peaceful places—his apartment, his shop, a café on a quiet street—some part of him remains in that convoy, listening for the next explosion.

Over time, he becomes aware that he is living in a state of constant alarm. He feels distant from other people, as if there is a pane of glass between him and the rest of the world. He can function, can work, can make conversation, but the effort of appearing normal leaves him drained. What stands out in the sessions is how much of his life has become organized around preventing the return of what has already happened, and how the memory of the war still shapes the way he sits, listens, moves, and waits.
